text: Server: versioned DB migration mechanism before the next schema change

Groomed (2026-07-14): re-prioritized p3 -> p2 and marked ready/agent — this
is now a common enabler, not an isolated nice-to-have. Two new tickets need
real schema changes: T-62 (lists.notes) and T-64 (items.last_touched_by_*,
account_settings.initials). Both were deliberately written to NOT hard-block
on this ticket (each bundles its own one-off, guarded ALTER TABLE so it can
ship independently either order) — but doing this one FIRST is the better
sequencing if there's no reason to rush T-62/T-64: it means those two land
using the real versioned mechanism instead of a bespoke one-off each, no
throwaway migration code, no risk of the "next real schema change" (T-57's
own stated trigger) arriving before this does.

If T-62 or T-64 ends up shipping first anyway (their one-off ALTER TABLEs
are safe to do so), fold those two migrations into this ticket's ordered
list retroactively when it lands, so schema_version accurately reflects
every column that's actually out there on deployed databases.

Done in f77220e. Used SQLite's built-in PRAGMA user_version instead of a
separate schema_version table (the ticket's original wording) — same
guarantee, simpler, and avoids the bootstrap problem of querying a version
table before it exists on a brand-new file.

migrations.py: ordered (version, [sql]) list, empty for now (CURRENT_VERSION
0) — ships the mechanism, not a migration. connect() applies pending
migrations whenever the database already has a meta table (the production
path: create_blueprint()'s per-request connect() never calls init_db(), so
this is what makes a live deployment self-heal its schema after a wheel
upgrade with zero operator action). init_db() stamps CURRENT_VERSION
directly on a truly fresh file (schema.sql already reflects every
migration) but still runs pending migrations if called against an existing
older database (app.py's dev server calls init_db() on every startup, even
against an already-populated dev.db). Each migration is one transaction;
a failure rolls back without advancing user_version, so a corrected retry
still applies. 4 new tests in test_db.py cover fresh-stamp, existing-DB
catch-up, no-reapply, and rollback-on-failure.

T-62 and T-64 each append one migration entry when implemented.
